subject: Copywriting
title: Apple: Think Different
description: A fast breakdown of Apple: Think Different for builders.

hook.text: In 1997, Apple was 90 days from bankruptcy. Steve Jobs came back and launched 'Think Different.' It was a resurrection.

buildup.text: The campaign showed Einstein, Lennon, MLK—no products. It told rebels they belonged at Apple. Identity before features.

discovery.text: Apple stock rose 33% within a year of the campaign.

twist.text: Grammatically, it should be 'Think Differently.' The deliberate error made it more memorable and reinforced rebellion.

climax.text: The slogan made Apple a lifestyle brand.

punchline.text: Two words saved a company. Think Different made Apple a religion.

quiz.question: What was Apple's financial state when 'Think Different' launched?

details.summary: Apple's 'Think Different' campaign, launched in 1997, repositioned Apple as the brand for creative rebels. Created by TBWA\Chiat\Day with Steve Jobs's direct involvement, the slogan celebrated nonconformists and became one of the most iconic brand statements in history.
details.whyItMatters: Think Different saved Apple from near-bankruptcy by redefining what the brand stood for. It proves that a great slogan can reshape an entire company's identity and destiny.
takeaways: Think Different positioned Apple as a brand for creative outsiders
The campaign featured icons like Einstein, Gandhi, and Picasso
Steve Jobs personally drove the creative direction of the slogan

faq.question: Is 'Think Different' grammatically correct?
faq.answer: Technically 'Think Differently' would be grammatically standard, but 'Think Different' uses 'different' as a flat adverb — the same construction as 'think big' or 'think fast.' The slight rule-breaking reinforces the slogan's rebellious message.

faq.question: How did Think Different change Apple's fortunes?
faq.answer: When Jobs returned to Apple in 1997, the company was weeks from bankruptcy. Think Different rallied employees and customers around a new identity. It set the cultural stage for the iMac, iPod, and everything that followed.
